n: A good reputation is worth more than expensive perfume. And the day of death, when a life is complete, can be better than the day of birth, when everything is still uncertain.
A funeral teaches more than a party, because it reminds us that everyone will die. The living should take that lesson to heart.

f.g: Take it seriously; reflect on it.

n: Sorrow can do more good than laughter, because sadness can soften and improve the heart.
The wise think seriously about death and life’s meaning, while fools think only about fun.
It is better to accept correction from a wise person than to listen to the songs and flattery of fools.
A fool’s laughter is like thorns crackling under a cooking pot — loud, quick, and soon gone, producing little heat.

f.w: crackling of thorns under a pot

n: Being oppressed can drive even a wise person to act foolishly, and bribes corrupt the heart.
The end of a matter is better than its beginning, and patience is better than pride. Waiting to see how things turn out is wise.
Don’t be quick to get angry; anger settles in the heart of fools.

f.w: hasty in thy spirit to be angry

n: Don’t ask why the “good old days” were better than today. That question isn’t wise; every age has its blessings and trials.
Wisdom is as valuable as an inheritance, and it benefits everyone who lives under the sun.
Both wisdom and money offer protection, but wisdom has the greater advantage: it preserves life itself.
Think about how God works: no one can straighten what He has allowed to be bent. Some trials must simply be accepted.
When times are good, be glad; when times are hard, stop and reflect. God allows both so people cannot predict the future and must trust Him.
In his life he has seen good people die young and wicked people live long. Life does not always seem fair in the short run.
Don’t be self-righteous or a know-it-all. Pride in one’s own goodness or wisdom can ruin a person.

f.g: Likely means self-righteous or showily pious, not truly good.

n: Nor should you plunge into wickedness or foolishness, which can bring an early death.
Hold on to both warnings. The person who reverences God will avoid both extremes.
Wisdom gives a person more strength than ten powerful rulers in a city.
Everyone sins; there is no one on earth who always does good. This is why all people need God’s mercy.

f.w: there is not a just man

n: Don’t pay attention to every word people say, or you may overhear even your servant criticizing you.
After all, you know you have criticized others yourself. Be forgiving of what others say.
He tested all this with wisdom and resolved to be truly wise, but full wisdom stayed beyond his reach.
The deepest truths are far off and profoundly deep — who can discover them? Only God fully understands.
He set himself to understand wisdom and the reasons behind things, and also the wickedness and madness of foolish living.

f.g: The sum or explanation of things.

n: He found something worse than death: the seductive woman of Proverbs whose love is a trap. Those who please God escape her; the sinner is caught.
The Preacher says he weighed things one by one, trying to reach a final total.

He kept searching but found few truly upright people — one in a thousand men, and among the women he dealt with, none. Many read this as reflecting his own life (compare 1 Kings 11:3), not a judgment on all women.

f.g: Solomon had a thousand wives and concubines (1 Kings 11:3), which may color this bitter remark.

n: His firm conclusion: God made people upright, but they have devised many schemes of their own. The problem lies in human choices, not in God’s creation.
